etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English eradicaten (“to eradicate”), from eradicat(e) (“eradicated”, past participle of eradicaten) +‎ -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin ērādīcātus, the perfect passive participle of ērādīcō (“to uproot, root out; to anihilate, eradicate”), from ē- (“out”) + rādīx (“root”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also radish.
senses: (transitive, now rare) To pull up by the roots.
(transitive) To destroy completely; to reduce to nothing radically; to put an end to.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: From Middle English eradicat(e) (“eradicated”, past participle of eradicaten), used up until Early Modern English, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.
